title: What Apollo’s choices reveal
source_text: Νυνὶ δὲ ὁ θαυμαζόμενος παρ᾿ Ἕλλησι Πύθιος οὐδένα μὲν σοφὸν ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ὅλως ἄνδρα ἄξιον ἔκρινε τῆς, ὡς Ἕλληνες ὑπολαμβάνουσι, θείας κατακωχῆς. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ἐν τῷ θήλει γένει παρθένον τινὰ ἢ σοφὴν καὶ ἀπὸ φιλοσοφίας ὠφελημένην ἀλλά τινα γυναῖκα ἰδιῶτιν· τάχα γὰρ οἱ ἐν ἀνθρώποις κρείττονες βελτίους ἦσαν τῆς εἰς τὴν κατακωχὴν ἐνεργείας αὐτοῦ. ἔδει δὲ καὶ. εἴπερ θεὸς ἦν, τῇ προγνώσει αὐτὸν χρήσασθαι δελέατι, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, πρὸς τὴν ἐπιστροφὴν καὶ θεραπείαν καὶ ἠθικὴν κατόρθωσιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων· νυνὶ δὲ οὐδὲν ἡ ἱστορία τοιοῦτον παραδίδωσι περὶ αὐτοῦ. εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἀνδρῶν ἁπάντων Σωκράτην εἶπε σοφώτατον εἶναι, ἤμβλυνε τὸν ἔπαινον αὐτοῦ τὸ πρὸς τούτου λεγόμενον περὶ Εὐριπίδου καὶ Σοφοκλέους ἐν τῷ· σοφὸς Σοφοκλῆς, σοφώτερος δ᾿ Εὐριπίδης. τραγῳδιοποιῶν ουν σοφῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ λελεγμένων κρείττων εἶναι νομισθεὶς ὁ Σωκράτης, τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς σκηνῆς καὶ τῆς ὀρχήστρας τοῦ τυχόντος ἄθλου ἕνεκεν ἀγωνιζομένων καὶ ὅπου μὲν λύπας καὶ οἴκτους τοῖς θεαταῖς ἐμποιούντων ὅπου δὲ ἀσέμνους γέλωτας (τοιοῦτον γάρ τι βούλεται τὰ σατυρικὰ δράματα), οὐ πάνυ τι τὸ διὰ φιλοσοφίαν καὶ ἀλήθειαν ἐμφαίνει σεμνὸν καὶ διὰ σεμνότητα ἐπαινετόν. καὶ τάχα οὐ τοσοῦτον διὰ φιλοσοφίαν ἀνδρῶν εἶπεν αὐτὸν ἁπάντων σοφώτατον ὅσον διὰ τὰς θυσίας καὶ ἃς προσήνεγκε κνίσσας αὐτῷ τε καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς δαίμοσι. καὶ διὰ ταῦτα ἐοίκασι μᾶλλον ποιεῖν οἱ δαίμονες τὰ ἀξιούμενα ὑπὸ τῶν αὐτοῖς προσαγόντων ἢ διὰ τὰ ἔργα τῆς ἀρετῆς. διόπερ διαγράφων τὰ γινόμενα ὁ τῶν ποιητῶν ἄριστος Ὅμηρος καὶ διδάσκων, τίνα μάλιστά ἐστι τὰ πείθοντα τοὺς δαίμονας ποιεῖν ἃ βούλονται οἱ θύοντες, εἰσήγαγε τὸν Χρύσην, ἕνεκεν ὀλίγων στεφάνων καὶ μηρίων ταύρων καὶ αἰγῶν τυγχάνοντα ὧν ᾔτησε καθ᾿ Ἑλλήνων διὰ τὴν θυγατέρα, ἵνα λοιμώξαντες ἀποδώσειαν αὐτῷ τὴν Χρυσηΐδα. μέμνημαι δὲ παρά τινι τῶν Πυθαγορείων, ἀναγράψαντι περὶ τῶν ἐν ὑπονοίᾳ παρὰ τῷ ποιητῇ λελεγμένων, ἀναγνοὺς ὅτι τὰ τοῦ Χρύσου πρὸς τὸν Ἀπόλλωνα ἔπη καὶ ὁ ἐξ Ἀπόλλωνος ἐπιπεμφθεὶς τοῖς Ἕλλησι λοιμὸς διδάσκει ὅτι ἠπίστατο Ὅμηρος πονηρούς τινας δαίμονας, χαίροντας ταῖς κνίσσαις καὶ ταῖς θυσίαις, μισθοὺς ἀποδιδόναι τοῖς θύσασι τὴν ἑτέρων φθορὰν, εἰ τοιοῦτο οἱ θύοντες εὔχοιντο. καὶ ὁ „Δωδώνης“ δὲ „μεδέων δυσχειμέρου,“ παρ᾿ ᾧ εἰσιν οἱ προφῆται „ἀνιπτόποδες χαμαιεῦναι,“ ἀποδοκιμάσας τὸ τῶν ἀνδρῶν εἰς προφητείαν γένος ταῖς Δωδωνίσι χρῆται, ὡς καὶ ὁ Κέλσος παρέστησεν. ἔστω δέ τις τούτοις παραπλήσιος Κλάριος καὶ ἕτερος ἐν Βραγχίδαις καὶ ἄλλος ἐν Ἄμμωνος ἢ ὅποι ποτὲ γῆς μαντευόμενοι, πόθεν οὖν δειχθήσεται εἰ καὶ θεοὶ μέν εἰσιν οὐ δαιμόνια δέ τινα;
pass_a_gloss: But now the Pythian (Πύθιος) admired among Greeks judged (κρίνω) no wise man, nor at all any man (ἀνήρ), worthy of the divine possession (θεία κατακωχή), as Greeks suppose; nor in the female race a virgin or a wise (woman) benefited from philosophy, but some lay (ἰδιῶτις) woman; for perhaps the better (κρείττονες) among men were better than his activity (ἐνέργεια) toward possession. He ought also, if he were a god, to have used foreknowledge (πρόγνωσις) as bait (δέλεαρ), so to name it, toward the conversion (ἐπιστροφή) and healing (θεραπεία) and moral correction (ἠθικὴ κατόρθωσις) of men; but now history (ἱστορία) hands down nothing such about him. For even if he said Socrates was wisest of all men, the (thing) said before this (πρὸ τούτου) about Euripides and Sophocles blunted (ἀμβλύνω) his praise (ἔπαινος), in: 'wise Sophocles, wiser Euripides'. Socrates, then, thought better than tragedy-makers (τραγῳδιοποιοί) called wise by him, competing on the stage (σκηνή) and orchestra for the sake of a chance prize (ἆθλον), producing in spectators sometimes griefs and pities (λύπαι, οἶκτοι), sometimes indecent laughter (ἀσέμνοι γέλωτες) (for satyr dramas want something such), does not at all display what is venerable (σεμνός) through philosophy and truth and praiseworthy through venerableness (σεμνότης). And perhaps he called him wisest of all men not so much through philosophy as through the sacrifices and the fat-smoke (κνῖσα) which he offered to him and to the other demons (δαίμονες). And through these the demons seem rather to do what is asked by those bringing (offerings) to them than through the works of virtue. Therefore Homer, best of poets, describing what happens and teaching what most persuades the demons to do what the sacrificers wish, introduced Chryses, obtaining for a few garlands (στέφανοι) and thighs (μηρία) of bulls and goats what he asked against the Greeks for his daughter, that, struck by plague (λοιμώσσω), they might give back to him Chryseis. I remember, having read in one of the Pythagoreans who wrote about the things said in hidden sense (ὑπόνοια) by the poet, that the verses of Chryses to Apollo and the plague (λοιμός) sent upon the Greeks from Apollo teach that Homer knew some wicked (πονηροί) demons, rejoicing in fat-smokes and sacrifices, pay as wages (μισθοί) to those who sacrificed the destruction (φθορά) of others, if the sacrificers should pray for such. And the 'ruler (μεδέων) of wintry (δυσχείμερος) Dodona', at whom are the prophets 'with unwashed feet (ἀνιπτόποδες), ground-sleepers (χαμαιεῦναι)', rejecting (ἀποδοκιμάζω) the race of men for prophecy, uses the Dodonian women, as Celsus too set forth. Let there be someone like these, a Clarian, and another at Branchidae and another at (the shrine) of Ammon, or wherever on earth divining: whence then will it be shown that they are indeed gods and not some demons (δαιμόνια)?
pass_b_english: But as it is, the Pythian god admired among the Greeks judged no wise man, and indeed no man at all, worthy of what the Greeks suppose to be divine possession. Nor, even among the female sex, did he choose a virgin, or a wise woman who had profited from philosophy, but some ordinary woman. Perhaps the better sort among human beings were too good for his work of possession.

Again, if he were a god, he ought to have used his foreknowledge as a bait, so to speak, for the conversion, the healing, and the moral reform of men. But as it is, history hands down nothing of the kind about him. For even if he said that Socrates was the wisest of all men, he blunted that praise by what he said about Euripides and Sophocles, in the line: “Sophocles is wise, Euripides wiser.” So Socrates was judged better than tragic poets whom the god had called wise, men who compete on the stage and in the orchestra for some trifling prize, and who sometimes stir grief and pity in the audience and sometimes unseemly laughter (for that is what satyr plays aim at). Ranked above such men, Socrates is hardly shown to have the dignity that comes from philosophy and truth, a dignity worthy of praise.

And perhaps he called him the wisest of all men not so much for his philosophy as for the sacrifices and the smoke of burnt fat that he offered to him and to the other demons. And it is for these things, it seems, rather than for works of virtue, that the demons do what is asked by those who bring them offerings. That is why Homer, the best of the poets, describing what happens and teaching what chiefly persuades the demons to do what those who sacrifice want, brought in Chryses: for the sake of a few garlands and the thighs of bulls and goats, he obtained what he asked against the Greeks on account of his daughter, that they should be struck with plague and give Chryseis back to him (Homer, Iliad 1.37–42). I remember reading in one of the Pythagoreans, who wrote about what the poet said in a hidden sense, that Chryses’ words to Apollo, and the plague sent by Apollo upon the Greeks, teach that Homer knew that certain evil demons, who delight in the smoke of fat and in sacrifices, pay those who sacrifice with the ruin of others, if that is what the sacrificers pray for.

And “the lord of wintry Dodona,” at whose shrine are the prophets “with unwashed feet, who sleep on the ground” (Homer, Iliad 16.234–235), rejected the male sex for prophecy and uses the women of Dodona, as Celsus too has pointed out. Granted that there is someone much like these at Claros, another at Branchidae, another at Ammon’s shrine, or wherever on earth they give oracles: how then will it be shown that they are gods, and not some demons?

choices.choice: The oracle line ‘σοφὸς Σοφοκλῆς, σοφώτερος δ᾿ Εὐριπίδης’ belongs to the Delphic response usually completed with ‘ἀνδρῶν δ᾿ ἁπάντων Σωκράτης σοφώτατος’ (transmitted in the scholia on Aristophanes, Clouds 144, and Diogenes Laertius 2.37); exact source not certain enough for an inline citation. ‘τὸ πρὸς τούτου λεγόμενον’ is read as πρός with the genitive of agent (‘what was said by him’), matching ‘ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ λελεγμένων’ in the next clause; no emendation to πρὸ τούτου is needed, and the lines belong to one oracle, so ‘before’ is not rendered. ‘τοῦ τυχόντος ἄθλου’ rendered ‘some trifling prize’. ‘κνῖσσα’ rendered ‘smoke of burnt fat’. ‘ουν’ in the staged text read as οὖν. Chryses’ prayer is Homer, Iliad 1.37–42 (he appeals to having roofed/garlanded Apollo’s temple and burned thighs of bulls and goats); cited inline. ‘Δωδώνης μεδέων δυσχειμέρου’ and ‘ἀνιπτόποδες χαμαιεῦναι’ are Homer, Iliad 16.234–235 (Achilles’ prayer to Zeus of Dodona; the Selloi are his prophets); cited inline. The unnamed Pythagorean allegorist is not identified. ‘τὸ πρὸς τούτου λεγόμενον ... ἤμβλυνε τὸν ἔπαινον’ has the saying as subject; rendered with the god as subject (‘he blunted that praise by what he had said before’) for natural English, same sense. ‘ἀνδρῶν ... ἁπάντων σοφώτατον’ rendered ‘the wisest of all men’. No Scripture quoted.
'τὸ πρὸς τούτου λεγόμενον' read as agent ('what he said'), dropped unsupported 'before'
'τοῦ τυχόντος ἄθλου' now 'some trifling prize' (was 'whatever prize may come')
Socrates sentence corrected to the Greek: not shown to have the dignity that comes from philosophy and truth, a dignity worthy of praise
'καὶ διὰ ταῦτα' sentence reordered so the 'for these things rather than virtue' contrast is clear; 'For' corrected to 'And'
'savour' replaced with plain 'smoke of burnt fat' (twice); 'Celsus himself' corrected to 'Celsus too' (καὶ ὁ Κέλσος)
